title: Effect of ActiGraph’s LFE for Estimating Steps and Physical Activity Intensity
author: Yuri Feito
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.jfacjie

steps.title: Obtain participant consent
steps.instruction: Read and have each participant sign the informed consent form; ensure the procedure is approved by the Institutional Review Board.

steps.title: Measure weight and height
steps.instruction: Measure body weight (kg) and height (m) using a Tanita digital beam scale with height rod (Tanita Corporation of America, Inc.; Arlington Heights, IL) while participants wear light clothing (e.g., shorts and t‑shirt) and no shoes; calculate BMI from the measured weight and height.

steps.title: Distribute accelerometer and pedometer
steps.instruction: Provide each participant with an ActiGraph GT3X+ accelerometer (ActiGraph; Pensacola, FL) and a New‑Lifestyles NL‑800 pedometer (New‑Lifestyles, Inc.; Lees Summit, MO) during the first laboratory visit.

steps.title: Attach devices to waist belt
steps.instruction: Place a belt around the participant’s waist at hip level; secure the AG‑GT3X+ on the right side of the belt at the midline of the thigh and the NL‑800 pedometer on the left side aligned with the midline of the thigh.

steps.title: Validate pedometer step count
steps.instruction: Have the participant perform a 20‑step walk around the laboratory while a researcher manually counts steps; if the NL‑800 records steps within one step of the manual count, accept it; otherwise adjust monitor placement or replace the device, then repeat the test before sealing the device to blind the participant.

steps.title: Instruct participants on monitor wear
steps.instruction: Tell participants to wear the belt with both monitors attached for seven consecutive days during all waking hours, removing it only for water activities; advise them not to alter their typical daily activities.

steps.title: Provide activity log
steps.instruction: Give each participant an activity log to record a summary of daily activities and the times the belt is put on and removed each day.

steps.title: Collect devices and logs
steps.instruction: At the end of the seven‑day monitoring period, retrieve the accelerometer, pedometer, and completed activity logs from each participant.

steps.title: Download raw accelerometer data
steps.instruction: Upload the AG‑GT3X+ raw data recorded at 60 Hz using ActiLife software version 6.0.

steps.title: Convert data with normal and LFE filters
steps.instruction: Using ActiLife, convert the raw files to counts per minute in two separate files: one applying the normal filter (AG‑N) and one applying the low‑frequency extension filter (AG‑LFE).

steps.title: Determine wear time validity
steps.instruction: Apply the Troiano et al. wear‑time algorithm; define a valid day as a minimum of 10 hours of wear time; require each participant to have at least four valid days for inclusion in the final analysis.

steps.title: Classify activity intensity
steps.instruction: Apply established cut‑points to the counts‑per‑minute data: sedentary < 100 cpm; light 100–2,019 cpm; moderate 2,020–5,998 cpm; vigorous ≥ 5,999 cpm; combine moderate and vigorous into one MVPA variable.

steps.title: Compute daily averages
steps.instruction: Average across all valid days for each participant the AG‑measured step counts and minutes per day spent in sedentary, light, and MVPA; also calculate the average steps per day recorded by the NL‑800 pedometer.

steps.title: Conduct statistical analyses
steps.instruction: Using SPSS version 22 for Mac (SPSS, Inc.; Chicago, IL) with α = 0.05, perform: (a) Pearson product‑moment correlations between AG‑LFE, AG‑N, and NL‑800 steps/day; (b) repeated‑measures ANOVA for device/filter effects (AG‑LFE × AG‑N × NL‑800) on steps/day; (c) 2 × 3 repeated‑measures ANOVA for device (AG‑LFE vs AG‑N) by intensity category (sedentary, light, MVPA); (d) Bonferroni‑adjusted pairwise comparisons to locate significant differences; (e) calculate eta‑square (h²) for effect size; (f) construct Bland‑Altman plots to show device error variability; present all results as mean ± standard deviation.
